newsitem.title: INDONESIA: No surprise at collapse of vote for Indonesia PDI.
newsitem.headline: No surprise at collapse of vote for Indonesia PDI.

text.p: The collapse of the minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) in general elections this past week suprised few political observers after the party's weak showing during the election campaign.
Analysts said on Saturday that the government-backed ousting of Megawati Sukarnoputri, popular daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno, had clearly backfired.
With most of the votes from Thursday's national and local elections counted, the PDI's share had plunged to three percent from 15 percent in the last poll in 1992.
The ruling Golkar had won a sweeping 74.26 percent, up from 68 percent in 1992, and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) 22.7 percent, up from 17 percent.
The government and the military backed a rebel faction headed by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi to oust Megawati at a congress in the North Sumatran city of Medan last June.
"Under the leadership of Surjadi, the PDI is finished and it shows that the government has gambled on the wrong man," said political analyst and Megawati loyalist Muchtor Buchori.
He said her supporters were now debating whether to try and recapture the PDI leadership or go outside the tightly controlled political system and create a new grouping.
Megawati herself has not so far commented on the poll.

Ironically, Megawati had been selected to replace Surjadi for a five-year term in 1993. At the time, the government was apparently unhappy that Surjadi had managed to boost the PDI's vote share to 15 percent from nearly 11 percent in 1987.

Political analysts said the government's about turn last year appeared related to fears over Megawati's grass-roots popularity and possible challenge to President Suharto next year, when the 75-year-old leader is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term.
The government apparently regarded Surjadi as the lesser of two evils.

Megawati has fought back against her ouster, declaring it illegal and unconstitutional. But she has so far been unsuccessful in court actions and she and her supporters were barred from contesting Thursday's election.
She said she herself would not vote, and called on her supporters not to take part in the election campaign organised by the Surjadi wing of the PDI and not to vote for it.
Analysts said the result was a disaster for the party.

"The complete collapse of the PDI is no surprise. It was expected by all analysts as soon as Megawati was removed in June last year," said Gerry van Klinken, editor of the Australian-based Inside Indonesia magazine.

"If there is no problem with the vote counting, then the drastic drop in PDI votes is a major cause for concern," Surajdi told the official Antara news agency on Friday. Party rivals said his days as leader were numbered.
Despite her exclusion from the official election process, Megawati's name never left the headlines during the 27-day campaign.

Her supporters took to the streets with the Moslem-oriented PPP carrying her picture in violation of electoral rules and proclaiming an impromptu alliance with the PPP under the banner "Mega-Bintang". Bintang or star is the symbol of the PPP.

But the government in an embarassing move was forced to come out and ban the words "Mega-Bintang" from the campaign, drawing further attention to the quietly-spoken Megawati, who kept a low-profile during the campaign and stayed at home.
PDI rallies throughout the election campaign were marked by poor attendances with security forces sometimes outnumbering the often underage supporters.
"Surjadi was clearly seen as being put there by the government and his credibility was low," one diplomat said.
